title: Jianmu-Q: Bridging Quantum Field Theory and Quantum Hardware with AI Agents
authors: Xiaolin Wang, Xingyu Guo, Jinyang Li, Tianyin Li, Enke Wang, Lingxiao Wang, Hongxi Xing
abstract: Quantum computing offers a promising approach to non-perturbative simulations of quantum field theories, particularly for real-time dynamics and systems affected by the sign problem. Yet translating continuum field theories into quantum computations remains a challenging interdisciplinary task. Here we introduce \texttt{Jianmu-Q}, a multi-agent framework that transforms natural-language descriptions of quantum field theories into quantum simulation workflows. Specialized agents handle theoretical formulation, lattice discretization, qubit mapping, and circuit design, while physical consistency checks and independent numerical calculations provide validation throughout the workflow. We benchmark the framework on three field theories of increasing complexity: the $(1+1)$-dimensional Nambu--Jona-Lasinio and Schwinger models, and a $(2+1)$-dimensional $\mathbb{Z}_2$ gauge theory. Across these systems, noiseless quantum-circuit simulations converge toward independent exact-diagonalization and tensor-network results, while selected circuits are executed on IBM quantum hardware, demonstrating an end-to-end, validation-guided approach to quantum simulation of field theories.
summary: This paper presents Jianmu-Q, a novel multi-agent framework designed to automate the translation of natural-language Quantum Field Theory descriptions into executable quantum simulation workflows. It tackles the major hurdle of implementing QFT simulations on quantum hardware by handling theoretical formulation, lattice discretization, and circuit design sequentially. The framework demonstrates end-to-end validation by comparing results across multiple simulation methods and actual quantum hardware.
main_problem: The core challenge is bridging the gap between continuum Quantum Field Theory (QFT) descriptions and executable quantum circuits for non-perturbative simulations.
main_result: The authors introduce Jianmu-Q, a multi-agent framework that successfully automates the end-to-end process, benchmarking on models like NJL and Z2 gauge theory.
method: A specialized multi-agent workflow translates natural language QFT descriptions into quantum simulation workflows, involving lattice discretization, qubit mapping, and circuit design.
model_or_system: The framework is tested on various QFTs, including the (1+1)D Nambu-Jona-Lasinio and Schwinger models, and a (2+1)D Z2 gauge theory, which is mapped onto a dual lattice representation.
key_observables:
Quark condensate, $N+2$-point correlation functions, hadron dispersion relation, and the hadronic tensor $W_{\mu
u}(q)$.
important_parameters: The complexity increases across the tested theories; convergence is monitored by comparing results across different ansatz depths ($D$) and Trotter steps ($N_T$).
main_assumptions: The validation checks are performed for the finite lattice, not the continuum limit, and the process relies on the coordination of multiple specialized agents.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the overall Jianmu-Q workflow as a staircase from QFT theory to quantum hardware, detailing validation steps against ED and TN results. Figure 8 shows the dual lattice encoding for the Z2 gauge theory.
paper_structure: The paper details the multi-agent architecture, first by defining the problem (QFT to quantum circuit), then by applying it to specific models (NJL, Z2), and finally demonstrating the end-to-end validation process, including hardware execution.
why_interesting: The systematic, automated pipeline for translating complex, continuum QFT problems into concrete quantum circuit implementations is highly relevant for developing quantum algorithms for high-energy physics simulations.

FIG. 5. State preparation ansatz for the Schwinger model. Each horizontal line represents the ten-qubit register. The up- per circuit applies D layers of the ansatz VD(θ) = UD...U2U1 to each reference state |rχ⟩, with χ = Ω, h. Superscripts on the rotation gates specify the qubit indices on which they act, and each gate has an independent angle in each layer. The exchange gates Gj and the RZZ gates act on adjacent qubits in ascending order of j, followed by single-qubit RZ rotations. Each layer has 28 independent parameters and preserves the total electric charge Q.
